2.3 — Healing Pickups & the Max-Health Cap

You can gain wealth and lose health. Now you need a way to get health back — and the moment you add healing, you create a new kind of problem. Healing without a limit is not a feature, it is an exploit. Today you compare the potion against both things you have already built, then discover that a value with a ceiling needs a rule, not just arithmetic.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I heal, and how do I cap health at a maximum?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

I want a potion that heals me when I walk into it, and I want my health to stop at the maximum and never go over it — no matter how many potions I find.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Make the potion something the player can touchwhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat (the pickup recipe)
  2. Recognize the potion in the callbackwhat does this part do?Read: the OnTriggerEnter2D and CompareTag rows of this lesson's reference table
  3. Change the health valuewhat does this part do?Read: 2.2 — Spikes: Physics, Damage & Death
  4. Hold the value under its ceilingwhat does this part do?Read: the Mathf.Clamp, Mathf.Min, Mathf.Max and selection rows of this lesson's reference table
  5. Consume the potionwhat does this part do?Read: the Destroy row of this lesson's reference table
  6. Test it at the boundarywhat does this part do?Read: this lesson's Bug Hunt: Boundary Conditions

The split follows the life of one value: an object is created, touched, recognized, changes a number, and dies. Five of those six parts are things you have already built — which is why the lesson is about the one part that is new, the ceiling, rather than about potions.

The split is finished when each part can be looked up on its own: every part above names either a component, an API call, or a method you have already written. If a part needs the word "and" twice to describe it, it is two parts.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

In one line: what is the exploit that a potion without a ceiling creates?

The coin pickup in 2.1 was trigger, tag check, change a value, destroy. Which part of the potion is the same as the coin's tag check, and which part is the same as its destroy?

2.2 put damage inside a method that changes health, not inside the spike. Where does that put the health cap — in the potion, or in the method that changes the value?

Which part of this problem has no twin in 2.1 or 2.2 at all, and how do you know?

Comparative Thinking ~15 min

Good engineers do not design from nothing. When you meet a new mechanic, ask what you have already built that behaves like it:

ComparisonAnalysis
How is the potion like the coin? Both are pickups: trigger colliders, handled by OnTriggerEnter2D, and destroyed on contact so they cannot be taken twice. Almost all of your coin code is reusable.
How is the potion like the spike? Both change health — and health lives on PlayerController, exactly where your coin count lives.
How is the potion different from both? It raises a value that now has a ceiling. Without a rule, ten potions means ten times the health, and the game stops being a game.
There is no potion art in this project — you are going to make one. There is no Potion prefab, no Potion tag and no potion sprite in Assets/Artwork. So: pick a sprite you do have, and tint it with the Sprite Renderer's Color field so it cannot be mistaken for a coin. Create the tag yourself. Building a mechanic with borrowed art is called greyboxing, and it is what professionals do all day — the mechanic is the work; the art is a placeholder until someone draws the real thing.

The same goes for the world: nothing is a potion until you have built the object and dragged instances of it into the Overworld. The spec below ends with that step, and skipping it means a mechanic nobody can walk into.

Socratic: Similar, Different, and Why It Matters

  1. The potion reuses the coin's trigger, its callback, and its destroy. What is the only thing that genuinely differs?
  2. Without a ceiling, a player who collects ten potions has ten times the health. Which breaks first — the challenge, the economy, or the feedback the player gets?
  3. The rule "health must never exceed the maximum" has to live somewhere. Name two places it could live, and say which one keeps the rule true no matter which script calls the healing method.
  4. If a second healing source arrives in Unit 5 — a heart, a shrine, a level-up — is a ceiling check inside the potion script still enough? What does your answer say about where rules belong?
Read the Docs: The API for Bounding a Value ~15 min

This is the level-3 substitute for a walkthrough. The API is laid out below and the code is not: you write the file. Three tools can hold a number inside a range, and one selection statement is not a tool at all — it is the thing that can do what none of the three can.

APISignatureWhat you getWhat it costs
Mathf.Clamp int Mathf.Clamp(int value, int min, int max) — float overloads exist too Returns the value pushed inside the range. The only tool here that holds both ends in one call, and the integer overload means health never has to become a decimal. It hands back a number and nothing else. It cannot tell you a heal was wasted, and a lower bound of 0 will quietly swallow the negative that an overkill counter might have wanted to see.
Mathf.Min int Mathf.Min(int a, int b) Returns the smaller of the two — a ceiling in a single expression. One end only. Nothing in it stops a value running off the bottom, so spikes plus potions means a second tool beside it.
Mathf.Max int Mathf.Max(int a, int b) Returns the larger of the two — a floor, and the tool for "never below zero" on its own terms. The mirror of Min: no ceiling at all. Alone it caps nothing.
Selection — if / else if / else A statement, not a method. It returns nothing. Runs its block only when the condition is true, and can do more than one thing: change the value and print a message, or refuse the heal outright. More lines than a one-line expression, and it puts the rule at the call site rather than inside the method that owns the value — so the next healing source has to repeat it.
[SerializeField] private int A field declaration, not a call — the form you have used since 1.3. Class body, never inside a method. The name and the starting value are yours to choose. A named value that survives every frame and appears in the Inspector as the designer's tuning knob. A value is not a rule. Anyone with the Inspector can set maximum health below current health while the game runs, and nothing warns them — your cap has to be written so that stays survivable.
OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) Callback. Unity calls it; you never do. Fires on the first frame two shapes overlap. The parameter is the other object's collider. Triggers only. Make the potion solid and this callback never runs — the collision callback takes over instead.
Collider2D.CompareTag(string) bool CompareTag(string tag) Asks the engine whether the collider's GameObject carries that tag. Exact spelling, and the tag has to exist in the project first. It is asked of whichever object owns the collider, which is why the collider lives on the root.
Destroy(Object) void Destroy(Object obj) Removes the object at the end of the frame. It is final. If the potion should stay on the ground until the player needs it, this is the wrong tool.
Debug.Log(object) void Debug.Log(object message) Prints to the Console — the only feedback this game has until Unit 5. Text only, and it prints when you call it. A heal that is refused silently prints nothing unless you print it yourself.
Three facts a signature cannot carry. First, the two Mathf tools hand you back a value — nothing changes until you assign it to the field that holds health, and a call whose result you drop is a line that does nothing at all. Second, an if is the only option here that can report as well as bound: a method that returns a number has no way to say "refused". Third, Mathf.Clamp bounds both ends in a single call, which is why it is the tool people reach for, and why you should be able to name its cost before you pick it.

Predict Before Building

  1. Current health is 2, maximum health is 5, and a potion restores 3. Walk each tool in the table: what does health become, and which of them can tell you that part of the heal was wasted?
  2. A spike drives health down while a potion drives it up. Which tool covers both ends in one call, and which two leave an end open?
  3. Only one option in that table can print a message as well as change the value. Why can a method that returns a number not do that?
  4. If your lower bound is 0, have you also implemented death? What is the difference between "this value cannot go below zero" and "the player dies"?
  5. A designer asks for a version where health may go negative, because a negative number is how the game counts overkill damage. Which tool survives that request, and which two would have to be rewritten?
Build Lab: The Potion ~30 min

This one is on you, and there is no code in this section on purpose. Every piece of it is something you have already built once: a prefab with a trigger collider is 2.1, a method that changes health is 2.2, and a tag check is both. What is new is the decision — and the specification below names the file, the field, the method and the question to answer. The reference table names the API. The rest is yours.

Architectural specification: the prefab.
  • In the Hierarchy, right-click → 2D Object → Sprite. Name it Potion, then drag it into Assets/Prefabs so it becomes reusable. What is the difference between the object in the scene and the asset in the folder?
  • Which sprite will you use, and what Sprite Renderer Color tint makes it obviously not a coin at a glance?
  • Add a collider. Trigger or solid — and what is your reason? Which of the two things you built this unit does that make it most like?
  • You are about to create a tag that does not exist in this project. Where does the tag list actually live, and does the prefab need the tag or does one instance in the scene? How do you confirm the spelling before you write it in a string, and what happens if you get it wrong?
  • Nothing is placed in the world yet. With the prefab finished, drag at least two instances into the Overworld scene, somewhere you will walk — one to test against a damaged player, and one to test against a full-health player.
Architectural specification: the rule.
  • What field holds the maximum health? What type and starting value, and how is it different from the current-health field? Which of the two is the designer's tuning knob, and which one is game state?
  • Where exactly does the ceiling get applied — in the potion before it calls the player, or inside the method that changes health? Which of those cannot be bypassed by a future caller?
  • Which tool from the reference table did you choose, and what does your choice do that the other three cannot?
  • If you chose the tool that bounds both ends, what is the lower bound — and what does bounding at 0 mean for the death check you wrote in 2.2?
  • If you bounded only one end, name the check that stops a spike driving health below zero, and say which method it lives in.
Architectural specification: the trigger.
  • Which callback, and which tag check?
  • Which method on the player do you call, and do you pass a positive or a negative number? Why does one method have to serve both the spike and the potion?
  • Do you destroy the potion? Which object — the collider's GameObject, or your own?
  • What should happen when a player already at full health touches a potion: consume it, or leave it on the ground? Both are defensible. Pick one, and name the check your choice requires and where that check belongs.

The Healing Decision

  1. Which tool did you choose, and what does it cost you? A rule with no stated cost is not yet a decision.
  2. Where did you put the ceiling — and how would you find out it was in the wrong place, using only the potion and a spike?
  3. Your potion and your spike now call the same method with different signs. What would you have to duplicate if you gave them separate heal and damage methods?
  4. Health is the third piece of state in this game that has to survive from one frame to the next. Where does it have to be declared for that to be true, and which line of your own code proves it?
  5. You tinted borrowed art and invented a tag to make this mechanic real. What did the placeholder cost you, and what would have been lost by waiting for real art?

Save, press Play, and verify. Drop your health on a spike, then walk into a potion and confirm it comes back up. Then walk into another potion at full health and confirm your rule holds. Then set maximum health in the Inspector while the game is running, and see what your rule does when the ceiling moves underneath the value.

Bug Hunt: Boundary Conditions ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Set maximum health to 5 in the Inspector. Does your cap still hold, or did you hardcode the number 3 somewhere in your file?
  2. Change your comparison from greater-than to greater-than-or-equal, or the reverse. With health exactly at the maximum, what happens now — and how would you ever have noticed if you only tested from the middle?
  3. Forget to create the tag, then ask CompareTag about it anyway. What does Unity report, and why is a loud error better here than silence?
  4. Make the potion solid instead of a trigger. What does the player do when they walk into it, and does the heal still fire?
  5. Heal at full health under each tool in the table. Which one silently does nothing, and which ones could tell you the heal was wasted?
  6. Set maximum health below your current health while the game is running. What does your rule do — and is that a bug or a feature?
  7. Delete the Potion prefab asset from Assets/Prefabs and return to the scene. What happens to the instances you placed — and what does that tell you is waiting for you in 2.4?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Choosing a Bounding Tool

  1. Rewrite your ceiling using the two-sided tool from the reference table. Does one call replace two checks — and what did you have to be careful about when you made the switch?
  2. Implement your answer to "should a full-health player waste a potion?" Which check did you add, and where did you put it?
  3. Read the docs for the two single-ended tools. Which would you use if a designer said "health may go negative — that is how we count overkill damage"?
  4. Where else in this game will a value need a ceiling — a fire rate, a detection radius, a jump count, a coin total? Which tool would you reach for there, and is it the same one you chose here?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain how the potion is like the coin, like the spike, and unlike both
  • Create a prefab and a brand-new project tag from scratch, and place instances in the scene
  • Explain the overheal exploit, and which rule prevents it
  • Compare if, Mathf.Min, Mathf.Max and Mathf.Clamp, and defend the one you chose — including what it costs
  • Explain why the rule lives in the method that changes health rather than in the potion
  • Test at the boundary — health exactly at maximum — instead of only in the middle
  • Commit and push
